case_name: Zundel v. Liberal Party of Canada
text:
Ontario

Supreme Court

Zundel v. Liberal Party of
Canada

Date: 1999-01-22

Zundel

and

Liberal Party of
Canada and the Reform Party of Canada and the New Democratic Party of Canada
and the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada and the Bloc Québecois and the
Canadian Jewish Congress and Ronen and Manning and Chrétien and Duceppe and
Mackay and Boudria and White and Blaikie and Wayne and McDonough and Fry and
Gagliano

Ontario
Court (General Division), Chadwick J.
January 22, 1999.

(No. 98-CV-7845)

Douglas H. Christie and Barbara Kulaszka,
for plaintiff.

David Migicovsky, for Liberal Party of Canada.

Emanuel Montenegrino and Daniel J. Leduc,
for Reform Party of Canada.

Hugh Blakeney, for New Democratic Party.

Martin W. Mason, for Progressive
Conservative Party of Canada.

David Y. Dwoskin, for Bloc Quebecois.

Eric R. Williams, for Canadian Jewish
Congress.

Brian A. Crane, Q.C., for individual
named defendants.

[
1
]

CHADWICK J.:—The defendants have brought two motions, the first is
on behalf of the various named political parties pursuant to rule 21.01(3)(
b
)
[
Rules of Civil Procedure,
R.R.O. 1990, Reg. 194] for an order
dismissing the action as against them on the basis that political parties do
not have the legal capacity to be sued.

[
2
]

The second motion is by the named defendants, all members of
Parliament, who bring a motion pursuant to rules 21.01(1)(
b
) and
21.01(3) for an order striking out the statement of claim as against them, on
the basis that the statement of claim concerns the privileges of Parliament and
are not subject to review in the courts.

[
3
]

The plaintiff seeks the following relief:

(a) a declaration that the defendants
violated the plaintiff’s right to freedom of expression guaranteed under

s. 2(
b
)

of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
;
and
that such violation was not justified under
s. 1
of the
Charter
;

(b) against each of the defendants for
wrongfully and maliciously violating the plaintiff’s right to freedom of
expression with intent to injure him, general damages in the amount of $250,000
pursuant to
s. 24(1)
of the
Charter
;

(c) against each of the defendants for
conspiracy to injure the plaintiff, general damages in the amount of $250,000;

(d) against each of the defendant Members
of Parliament for public misfeasance and abuse of office, general damages of
$250,000; and

(e) against each of the defendants,
punitive damages in the amount of $500,000.

[
4
]

The facts on which the plaintiff relies are set out in the following
paragraphs of the statement of claim:

On or about June 3, 1998, the plaintiff announced by
Press Release that he was holding a press conference on Friday, June 5, 1998 in
person in Ottawa in the
Canadian Parliamentary Press Gallery’s Charles Lynch Press Conference Room in
Room 130 S Centre Block of the Parliament Buildings. Prior to issuing the press
release, the plaintiff had arranged and been granted time for the press
conference in the said room with the officials of the Canadian Parliamentary
Press Gallery.

The subject of the press conference was a
case before the Human Rights Tribunal in which the plaintiff was accused under
the
Canadian Human Rights Act,
section 13(1) of exposing Jews to
hatred and contempt on an Internet website known as the “Zundelsite” located in
the United States. The title of
the plaintiff’s press conference topic was “The New Inquisition in Toronto! Government tries to grab control
of the Internet”. The plaintiff intended to discuss the Tribunal’s ruling that
truth is not a defence under the legislation and the fact that the Canadian
Human Rights Commission was attempting to obtain jurisdiction over the Internet
in this precedent-setting case. The press release is attached to this Claim as
Schedule A.

The Canadian Parliamentary Press Gallery’s
press conference rooms are used for press conferences for issues of national
concern. The rulings of the Human Rights Tribunal which the plaintiff was going
to discuss at the press conference involved important matters for all Canadians
concerned with freedom of speech, the role of truth and intent in human rights
proceedings and the jurisdiction of the Canadian Human Rights Commission over
the Internet.

The plaintiff booked the Charles Lynch
Press Conference Room with the Canadian Parliamentary Press Gallery to give the
widest possible dissemination of his press conference to Canadians to alert
them to the rulings made by the Human Rights Tribunal and to the implications
of such rulings on Canadian society and the Internet.

On or about June 4, 1998, the defendants
wrongfully and maliciously conspired and combined amongst themselves to injure
the plaintiff by banning him from the precincts of Parliament, thereby
preventing him from holding a press conference in the Canadian Parliamentary
Press Gallery’s press conference rooms, and wrongfully violating his right to
freedom of expression under
section 2(b)
of the
Canadian Charter of
Rights and Freedoms
.

In pursuance and in furtherance of the said
conspiracy, the defendants did the following overt acts, namely:

(a) On or about June 4, 1998, the defendant Moshe Ronen,
National President of the defendant Canadian Jewish Congress, learned that the
plaintiff intended to hold a press conference to discuss the proceedings before
the Human Rights Tribunal on the following day.

(b) Meetings were held by the defendants
Moshe Ronen representing the defendant Canadian Jewish Congress, the defendant
Hedy Fry, the defendant Alfonso Gagliano and other ministers and Members of
Parliament for the purpose of deciding on a plan of action to wrongfully deny
the plaintiff his right to freedom of expression in the holding of a press
conference in the Centre Block Charles Lynch Press Conference room.

(c) The defendant party House Leaders Bill
Blaikie, Randy White, Peter MacKay and Don Boudria all rose in the House of
Commons later on June 4, 1998 to say they had learned of the plaintiff’s plans
to hold the press conference and to state that he must not be permitted to use
the Charles Lynch Press Conference room, Room 130-S, Centre Block given his
well-known position on the Holocaust. The defendant Don Boudria acknowledged
that the government did not administer the rooms in question and that the room
was in fact accessible to the plaintiff. Boudria stated he had contacted the
officials of the Press Gallery on Parliament Hill who administered the rooms
and expressed his dissatisfaction that the Parliament Buildings were going to
be utilized in any way, shape or form for the benefit of “one Ernst Zundel” to
host his press conference.

(d) The officials of the Canadian
Parliamentary Press Gallery refused to cancel the plaintiff’s booking of the
Charles Lynch Press Conference Room after being requested to by the defendants.
As a result the defendants conspired and agree [
sic
]

to pass a
motion banning the plaintiff from the precincts of the House of Commons during
and for the remainder of the Parliamentary session.

(e) Later in the day on June 4, 1998, the
defendant Don Boudria rose in the House of Commons and said: “Mr. Speaker,
I rise on a point of order pursuant to an issue raised earlier this afternoon
and well put by all House leaders. Pursuant to discussions held subsequently, I
now offer the following motion to the House and ask for unanimous consent that
it be passed immediately without debate. I move:

“That this House order that Ernst Zundel be
denied admittance to the precincts of the House of Commons during and for the
remainder of the present session”.

(f) The motion passed with the unanimous
consent and agreement of the defendants Liberal Party of Canada, the reform
Party of Canada, the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada, the Bloc
Québéçois and the New Democratic Party and of the defendant party leaders,
house leaders and members.

CAPACITY
TO BE SUED:

[
5
]

The political parties take the position that they have no legal
existence and therefore lack the capacity to sue or to be sued. Counsel for the
plaintiff argues that the political parties are all registered under the
Canada
Elections Act
, R.S.C. 1985, c. E-2 and as such have appointed a chief agent
which carries out all of the responsibilities of the political parties and the
political parties are in fact the principles giving instructions to the chief
agent. Reference is made to s. 31(11) of the
Canada Elections Act
which
reads as follows:

31. (11) The chief agent or registered
party that is deleted from the registry referred to in subsection 24(1)
shall, within three months after the expiration of the period referred to in
subsection (10), provide for the transmittal of the return, liquidate the
assets of the party, pay the debts of the party and remit any remaining balance
to the Chief Electoral Officer who shall transmit that balance to the Receiver
General or, where there is no balance remaining, so inform the Chief Electoral
Officer by a notice in writing.

[
6
]

In
McKinney
v. Liberal Party of
Canada

(1987),
1987 CanLII 4138 (ON HCJ)
, 35 C.R.R. 353, 61 O.R. (2d) 680
(S.C.), Gravely D.C.J. dealt with a similar motion. In that case an individual
voter brought an action against the three major political parties of Canada for
an injunction restraining them from exercising party discipline over their
members to the extent that this might prevent members of Parliament from voting
according to their consciences or their constituents’ wishes. He struck out the
plaintiff’s statement of claim on the basis that the political parties had no
capacity to be sued. In doing so, he relied upon the decision of the House of
Lords in
Taff Vale Railway Co. v. Amalgamated Society of Railway Servants,
[1901]
A.C. 426
. There it was found that a trade union registered under the relevant
trade union Acts could be sued in its registered name. At p. 436, Farwell
J., Earl of Halsbury L.C., stated as follows:

If the Legislature has created a thing
which can own property, which can employ servants, and which can inflict
injury, it must be taken, I think, to have impliedly given the power to make it
suable in a Court of Law for injuries purposely done by its authority and
procurement.

[
7
]

Lord Shand said at pp. 440-41:

It is true, as repeatedly stated both by
Farwell J. and by the Master of the Rolls, that by neither of the statutes are
trade unions, although registered, declared to be incorporations, which would
as a consequence give them a right to sue and render them liable to be sued in
the society’s name. It is equally true, as the Master of the Rolls observes,
that the right to sue and liability to be sued may be conferred by statute
either expressly or by implication. In the words of the learned Master of the
Rolls, enactments “must be found either express or implied enabling this to be
done”. I agree in thinking there is no express enactment to that effect; but,
with great deference, in my opinion the power of suing and liability to be sued
in the society’s name is clearly and necessarily implied by the provisions of
the statutes.

[
8
]

After reviewing the provisions of the
Canadian Elections Act
and
applying comments of the House of Lords in
Taff Vale,
Gravely D.C.J.
concludes at pp. 356-57 C.R.R., p. 683 O.R. as follows:

Is there anything in the legislation
affecting these political parties that necessarily implies their right to sue
and be sued in the name of the party? I do not think so. They are not given by
the legislation the right as in the
Taff Vale
case to hold property to
or to act generally by agents. The legislation is essentially regulatory. If
there is any inference to be drawn from the legislation, then I think the more
reasonable inference is that Parliament intended to confine the effect of the
legislation to its plain terms.

[
9
]

The decision in
McKinney v. Liberal Party of Canada

was
subsequently followed in
Monroe v.

Canada,
[1993] O.J. No. 2370

by Borins J.

[
10
]

Counsel for the plaintiff argues that the laws
have developed so that unincorporated associations or organizations can now sue
or be sued in their own names. He notes that Gravely D.C.J. did not consider
that when giving his reasons in
McKinney
.
In support of his proposition he
relies upon
Warkentin v. Sault Ste. Marie Board of Education
(1985), 49
C.P.C. 31, [1985] O.J. No. 1616 (Dist. Ct.)
. Vannini D.C.J. dealt with the motion where the plaintiffs were
being prevented from playing senior boys high school basketball on the basis
that the local association had declared the plaintiffs ineligible to play. At
p. 5 O.J. of his reasons, he states as follows:

It was once well-established that an
unincorporated association or organization was not in law a judicial person and
could not sue or be sued in its name. In recent years, however, and more
particularly in the field of organized athletic activities by unincorporated
associations, the law has advanced considerably to the extent of recognizing
that an association may properly be named as a party in an action by its name,
either as a plaintiff to enforce a right or as a defendant in defence of an
action arising out of the rules of a particular athletic activity as set out in
the constitution of the association: see Hanson v. Ontario University Athletic
Association (1975),
1975 CanLII 489 (ON HCJ)
, 11 O.R. (2d) 193, Toronto Marlboros Junior A Hockey Club v.
Tonelli (1976),
1975 CanLII 517 (ON HCJ)
, 11 O.R. (2d) 664; Chantler v. Metropolitan Toronto Hockey
League
(1983), 43 O.R. (2d) 85
; Holmes v. Metro. Toronto Hockey League, Ont.
H.C., J. Holland J., February 17, 1984 (unreported); Sheddon v. Ontario Major
Junior Hockey League, (1978),
1978 CanLII 1673 (ON HCJ)
, 19 O.R. (2d) 1,; Hebert v. Shawinigan Cataracts
Hockey Club (1978),
1978 CanLII 1339 (ON HCJ)
, 22 O.R. (2d) 654); Greenlaw v. Ont. Major Jr. Hockey
League, Ont. H.C., Montgomery J., August 22, 1984 (unreported). Gretzky v. Ont.
Minor Hockey Assn. (1975),
1975 CanLII 508 (ON HCJ)
, 10 O.R. (2d) 759, Cummings and Ontario Minor Hockey Association, Re
(1978),
1978 CanLII 1551 (ON HCJ)
, 21 O.R. (2d) 389.

Based upon the precedents established by
these authorities, I do not hold that an unincorporated athletic association
may be a party in the name of the association in a proceeding either as an
applicant or a plaintiff or as a respondent or a defendant.

[
11
]

In the case at bar, the plaintiff is not a
member of any of the named political parties. That alone distinguishes him from
the positions of the plaintiffs in
Warkentin.

[
12
]

The fact that the
Canada Elections Act
provides
for the chief agents to conduct affairs on behalf of the political parties does
not vest the political parties with the capacity to sue or be sued. The
Canada
Elections Act
does not go that far to provide them with that right and
responsibility. It is common ground by counsel for all of the political parties
that the political parties have no assets, hold no real estate, employ no
people, and as such are not a legal entity. I agree with their position and on
that basis I would dismiss the claim as against the political parties.

[
13
]

On the motion by the named defendants who are
all members of Parliament, the onus is on them to establish the plaintiff could
not possibly succeed at trial. The court must proceed with caution in analyzing
a statement of claim at this early stage which could result in the plaintiff
being denied his right to a trial. Applying the law it must be clearly settled
by binding authority that the plaintiff has no cause of action: see
Hunt v.
Carey Canada Inc.,
1990 CanLII 90 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 S.C.R. 959, 74 D.L.R. (4th) 321 at pp. 333 and
334.

[
14
]

Mr. Christie on behalf of the plaintiff
Ernst Zundel does not take issue with the exercise of parliamentary privilege
but does question whether in this case the resolution denying Mr. Zundel
the right to use the precinct of Parliament for a speech was necessary to the
proper functioning of Parliament. In support of his position, he relies upon
the decision in
Harvey
v.
New Brunswick
(Attorney General)
(1996),
1996 CanLII 163 (SCC)
, 37 C.R.R.
(2d) 189, [1996] 2 S.C.R. 876. In that case the appellant had been
elected to the New Brunswick Legislative Assembly in 1991. After the election,
he was convicted of illegal practice under the
Canada Elections Act
and
was expelled from the Legislature. At trial, he was successful in challenging
the provisions of the
Canada Elections Act
which was overturned on
appeal. On appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada, amongst other things, the
court considered the question of parliamentary privilege and the courts and in
her minority judgment, McLachlin J. at p. 218 C.R.R., p. 917 S.C.R.
states:

Because parliamentary privilege enjoys constitutional
status it is not “subject to” the
Charter
,
as are ordinary laws. Both
parliamentary privilege and the
Charter
constitute essential parts of
the Constitution of Canada. Neither prevails over the other. While
parliamentary privilege and immunity from improper judicial interference in
parliamentary processes must be maintained, so must the fundamental democratic
guarantees of the
Charter.
Where apparent conflicts between different
constitutional principles arise, the proper approach is not to resolve the
conflict by subordinating one principle to the other, but rather to attempt to
reconcile them.

[
15
]

Further at pp. 218-19 C.R.R., p. 918
S.C.R.:

This is not to say that the courts have no
role to play in the debate which arises where individual rights are alleged to
conflict with parliamentary privilege. Under the British system of
parliamentary supremacy, the courts arguably play no role in monitoring the
exercise of parliamentary privilege. In Canada, this has been altered by the
Charter
’s
enunciation of
values which may in particular cases conflict with the exercise of such
privilege. To prevent abuses cloaked in the guise of privilege from trumping
legitimate
Charter
interests, the courts must inquire into the
legitimacy of a claim of parliamentary privilege. As this court made clear in
New Brunswick
Broadcasting, the
courts may properly question whether a claimed privilege exists.
This screening role means that where it is alleged that a person has been
expelled or disqualified on invalid grounds, the courts must determine whether
the act falls within the scope of parliamentary privilege. If the court
concludes that it does, no further review lies.

British jurisprudence distinguishes between
privileges asserted by resolution and privileges effected automatically by
statute. In respect of privileges asserted by resolution, British courts have
developed a doctrine of necessity, enabling them to inquire whether the action
taken by resolution is necessary to the proper functioning of the House. The
necessity inquiry does not ask whether the particular action at issue was
necessary, and hence does not involve substantive judicial review. Rather, it
asks whether the dignity, integrity and efficiency of the legislative body
could be maintained if it were not permitted to carry out the type of action
sought to be done, for example to expel a person from the Legislature or
disqualify a person from seeking office on grounds of corruption. Following
this rule, this court in
New Brunswick Broadcasting
inquired whether the
resolution there in issue was necessary to the proper functioning of the
Legislature and the maintenance of its integrity. The question was left open
whether a similar inquiry should be conducted where a legislated privilege,
like the one asserted in the case at bar, is in question.

[
16
]

The
Harvey

decision followed and
incorporated the previous decision by the Supreme Court of Canada in
New
Brunswick Broadcasting Co. v. Nova Scotia (Speaker of the House of Assembly)
(1993),

1993 CanLII 153 (SCC)
, 13 C.R.R. (2d) 1, [1993] 1 S.C.R. 319. In the
New Brunswick Broadcasting Co.

case the court upheld the right of the Nova Scotia Legislature to control
and prohibit the use of television cameras in the House of Assembly. The court
confirmed that the test of necessity for privileges is a jurisdictional test
and pointed out the need, in each case, to determine whether a particular
matter falls within the necessary spear of matters without which the dignity
and efficiency of the House cannot be upheld. That case is authority for the
fact that the courts should look at claims of privilege where they are close to
the line as is suggested in the case at bar. At p. 38 C.R.R., p. 350
S.C.R., the court states:

Another general proposition which can be
derived from the case law is that the courts are apt to look more closely at
cases in which claims to privilege have an impact on persons outside the
Assembly than at those which involve matters entirely internal to the Assembly.
The lines are not altogether clear here either though. For example, in the case
before us the issue clearly revolves around the internal proceedings of the
Assembly. At the same time, it is persons not connected to the Assembly who
allege their rights are infringed. Does this qualify as a “inside case” or as a
“outside case”?

[
17
]

It cannot be argued that Ernst Zundel was
interfering with Parliament by booking a room in the House of Commons.
Mr. Zundel was a stranger to the House and as such the actions of the
House must be looked at with closer scrutiny. It is argued that the resolution
of the House has interfered with the plaintiff’s rights to freedom of speech as
guaranteed to him by the
Charter
.
The unanimous motion which was passed
in the House of Commons without debate moved by Don Boudria is as follows:

That this House order that Ernst Zundel be
denied admittance to the precinct of the House of Commons during and for the
remainder of the present session.

[
18
]

In my view, the House of Commons was exercising
its parliamentary privilege in restricting the precincts of the House of
Commons being used by the plaintiff Ernst Zundel. I am also satisfied it meets
the test of necessity and therefore the court should not interfere with the
decision of Parliament. In arriving at that conclusion, I note the restriction
placed upon the plaintiff was only the use of the precincts of the House of
Commons and not prohibition from speaking. Although there is no reference to
the reason behind the decision, it is obvious it was to preserve the dignity
and integrity of Parliament.

[
19
]

Likewise the claim against the named members of
Parliament for conspiracy is also protected by privilege. In
Roman Corp. v.
Hudson’s Bay Oil & Gas Co.,
1971 CanLII 499 (ON HCJ)
, [1971] 2 O.R. 418 at p. 422, 18 D.L.R.
(3d) 134 (H.C.J.) Holden J. made the following comment relating to privilege
and immunities provided to members of the House of Commons. At p. 423
O.R., he states:

The Court has no power to inquire into what
statements were made in Parliament, why they were made, who made them, what was
the motive for making them or anything about them:
R. v. Bunting
(1885),
7 O.R. 524 [
sic
]

p. 544
;
Dillon v. Balfour
(1887), 20 L.R.
Ir. 600 at pp. 625-6;
Stockdale v. Hansard
(1839), 9 Ad. & E. 1 at
pp. 114 and 209, 221 E.R. 1112
;
Erskine
May,
Parliamentary Practice,
16th
ed., at p. 48
et seq.
The defendants Trudeau and Greene could not
be made to give evidence as to what happened in the House without the
permission of the House of Commons:
Chubb v. Salomons
(1852), 3 Car.
&

K. 75, 175 E.R. 469
. On the basis of the foregoing, it seems to be
well established that no person can have a judgment awarded against him in
civil proceedings arising out of a speech made in the House of Common [
sic
]

and, therefore, para. 10 and the second sentence of para. 13 must
be struck out.

[
20
]

For these reasons the statement of claim as against
the named defendants Preston Manning, Jean Chrétien, Gilles Duceppe, Peter
MacKay, Don Boudria, Randy White, Bill Blaikie, Elsie Wayne, Alexa McDonough,
Hedy Fry and Alfonso Gagliano will be struck out as not establishing any
reasonable cause of action.

[
21
]

I will receive written submissions from counsel
with reference to the question of costs, both as to fixing costs and the amount
of costs to be fixed. The submissions to be received within 15 days of the
release of these reasons.

Motions granted.
